articles.title: Trump holds press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
articles.summary: Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips.
body: President Trump touted his recent trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin during a White House press conference Friday, saying the U.S. took the stage from a position of strength.
"The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," he said, though the historic summit between the three countries yielded few tangible results.
Watch the 12 p.m. ET news conference live:
Trump, flanked by Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, noted that oil prices have been dropping and noted that those prices are closely tied to how things are going in Iran.
"They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me. We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they've been doing for 51 years," he said.
Trump also said he and Chinese President Xi were agreeing to "joint guardrails" amid the race to develop artificial intelligence, a notable acknowledgement about the risks involved.

Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."
Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S.

"Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off. And there's always somebody else in this country. But if it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.

Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.

Ahead of the press conference, Trump said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.

Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.
While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.

"The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."

Foreign trips are often largely about the pomp and circumstance involved in meetings between heads of state. Among other special events, Trump's arrival in China, for example, included a military flyover and young dancers.

But the events are also extensively choreographed, with aides working months in advance to lock down agreements and commitments that the leaders can point to as evidence of a successful trip. That did not appear to be a main objective for this visit.
For Xi, he was able to boast of China's global leadership by bringing together the world's greatest nuclear powers to discuss global challenges.
For Putin, the meeting allowed a chance to reestablish Russia as a great geopolitical power on par with China and the U.S.
And for Trump, it's a chance to turn the page and demonstrate his ongoing power at a time when he's been weakened domestically after the devastating midterm elections.
In his opening remarks alongside Xi and Putin, Trump said the three leaders were making history and that they had a responsibility to the rest of the world to maintain open and respectful dialogue.

"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite," Trump said. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech."
But while the kind words and pats on the back were prevalent, the lack of deliverables was also noteworthy.
It has raised questions about Trump's approach to foreign policy.

Trump has spent much of the last few years trying to replace the postwar rules-based order, ripping up traditional alliances in favor of a more personal approach to diplomacy. He prefers to work out deals personally with the world's superpowers.
But the visit may be demonstrating that access does not always produce results.

Xi and Putin have their own strategic objectives, which are not going to change because they're friendly with Trump. As Maloney put it, they also have to calculate whether agreements reached with Trump can survive domestic scrutiny or a change of administration in the coming years.

"I think both Putin and Xi recognized that President Trump's time is beginning to wane," Maloney said, "that his command of U.S. politics is also beginning to wane, and they're going to be looking to who and what may be coming next."

articles.title: Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa
articles.summary: Congress needs to pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown next month, providing Dems an opportunity to leverage power. And, the Army says waiting to detonate lead azide could become dangerous.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.

The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.

Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

articles.title: GOP Sen. Johnson rejects tying government funding to an end to the Iran war
articles.summary: "We're not going to shut down the war," Sen. Ron Johnson said as Republicans and Democrats struggle to reach a government funding deal.
body: Republican Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who has defended President Trump's war with Iran, said Friday that he opposes tying government funding to an end to the conflict as Congress struggles to avert a shutdown before Christmas.
"We're not going to shut down the war. That is President Trump's power. He's exercising his constitutional authority," Johnson, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, told Morning Edition.

Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to keep federal agencies operating, giving Democrats leverage in the Republican-controlled Senate, where most legislation requires 60 votes to advance. But both parties face divisions. Democrats disagree over whether to use the funding deadline to force an end to the war, while Republicans are weighing bipartisan negotiations against a party-line approach to securing additional military spending.

Johnson said Republicans would prefer to negotiate a spending agreement with Democrats rather than use budget reconciliation, a procedure that could allow them to approve defense funding without Democratic support.
"I think we'll give them one more chance," he said, referring to negotiations before the Thanksgiving recess.

Johnson, who previously supported military aid to Ukraine but later opposed additional funding, warned that temporary spending measures would hinder military modernization and weapons procurement. He pointed to the changing nature of warfare in Ukraine as an example.

A shutdown could furlough hundreds of thousands of federal workers or delay their pay just weeks before Christmas. Johnson said he hoped to avoid one but warned that Republicans would need Democratic support.

The war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran has killed thousands of people, threatened U.S. military bases across the region and become a point of contention in the American midterm elections. Asked what he wanted to see happen in Iran, Johnson said he hoped Iranians would rise up against their government and that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.
"I want to see the Ayatollahs on the dustbin of history," he said.

articles.title: The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
articles.summary: A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences.
body: BRUSSELS — A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be "a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security."
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be signed Friday as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people."
He said "a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe."
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.

There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain's economy.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain's independence.

"I'm afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again," Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said "it's perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?"

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.'s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

"Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential," Costa said ahead of the meeting. "By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond."

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country's intentions.

Ireland's ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, "there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant." If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must "make a clear decision as to what it wants."

articles.title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
articles.summary: The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar security forces "acted with genocidal intent" against the Rohingya during military operations in the northern Rakhine state in 2017.
body: The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.

Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."

For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.

The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.

Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."

"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."

Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.

"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.

The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.

Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.

The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.

However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.

Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.

"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.

She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.

Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra is an ensemble founded by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim nearly 30 years ago in Germany to unite Middle Eastern musicians. articles.title: Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
articles.summary: Rep. Gregory Meeks raises concerns about U.S. alliances after Trump's summit with Xi and Putin. He also discusses Chinese espionage amid the Nvidia scandal.
body: Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.
"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.

His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.

Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.
Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.
"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.

Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.summary: President Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin have gathered in Shenzhen, China, for a historic trilateral meeting, with Ukraine, Iran and nuclear disarmament on the agenda.
body: SHENZHEN, China, and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday. Their meeting capped two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," Xi said in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders laying out divergent agendas going in:

Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to smuggle in high-end Nvidia chips.

In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.

Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."

Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.

The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.

For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.

Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.

Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.

Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.

In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.

Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.

Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.

Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."

Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.
Additional research by Jasmine Ling.

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
articles.summary: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.
body: Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
articles.summary: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
body: Watch: Miliband says tuition fees for EU students are a 'separate issue'

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
articles.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
body: The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles.summary: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
body: Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

articles.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
articles.summary: Earlier this week, Trump greeted Putin ahead of a meeting in China and said the pair have a "great relationship.
body: Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has labelled Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

On the sidelines of a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin on Thursday, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations on Friday, days after Ukraine badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the southeast of the country early on Friday.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said one missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The missile hit about 100km (62 miles) from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the Coalition of the Winning - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

articles.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
articles.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
body: Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu and French author investigated over sexual allegations
articles.summary: A judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed last year over "allegations of a sexual nature".
body: Michel Houellebecq (left) and (right) Gérard Depardieu have been accused of an on-set incident
Warning: this story contains graphic content
French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.
The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.
The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.
Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.

The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.
She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".
French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.

The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.
Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".
The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.
The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.
On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.
Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.

articles.title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
articles.summary: Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
body: Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years

New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.
Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.
He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.
Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.
The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
body: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

articles.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
articles.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
body: Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
articles.summary: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
body: Nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.
Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.
He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.
Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.
The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."
Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader
Who was Canadian Sikh leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar?
Why are some Sikhs calling for a separate state?
Canada accuses India of role in Sikh leader's murder

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.
"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

articles.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
articles.summary: Police officials called for "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
body: The killing of 13 women around Johannesburg earlier this year sparked a national outcry
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.
This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.
The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.
In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.
The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.
The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.
Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.

It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.
Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.
The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.
The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.
On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.
General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.
The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.

The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.
He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.
Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.
In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings.
Last year, he declared that violence against women was a "national disaster".

articles.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
articles.summary: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.
body: Reinaldo Dennes was convicted over the murder of a diamond dealer in 1996
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.
This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.
His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.
Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.
When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".
He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."
Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.
"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?

The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murderer, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.
Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.
