articles.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
articles.summary: Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner
body: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.
Related: UN warns against misuse of security laws as UK weighs Palestine Action ban

Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.
Related: Britain’s veto could stop the UAE’s choice from running the United Nations. Miliband must use it | Steve Bloomfield

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner
articles.summary: US envoy also says he believes Moscow is ‘comfortable’ with a guarantee; Russia attacks Kyiv bridges after Putin vows response for Crimea bridge attack. What we know on day 1,731
body: US envoy Jared Kushner has said Donald Trump is open to extending Ukraine a security guarantee similar to Nato’s mutual defence clause, but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Kyiv’s allies to “reopen the question” of Ukraine becoming a member of the military alliance. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, told a press conference in Germany: “From America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. We also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.”

Kushner’s comments came after Ukraine’s allies gathered for a summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelenskyy to emphasise support for Kyiv nearly five years since Russia’s 2022 invasion, and to push for a European role in future peace negotiations. Kushner added on Thursday that “we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5 ”. He noted that went with Moscow’s intention to “not have another war” when this conflict was over, while acknowledging “scepticism” over the position.

Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to do the “maximum” to deliver the air defence systems it needed, as well as looking again at Ukraine joining Nato. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to Nato,” the French president said in Berlin. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.

Vladimir Putin said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea would be “painful”, after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week. The Russian president claimed he had considered agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed, report Dan Sabbagh and Jakub Krupa.

On Friday, after Putin’s threat, a Russian ballistic missile attack hit three ⁠bridges on Kyiv’s Dnipro River and killed three people, the city’s mayor said, in the ⁠biggest strikes on routes ⁠connecting ​the left and right banks of Ukraine’s capital since the war began. The missiles hit the ⁠Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges, Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or ⁠traffic restrictions. About ‌15 people were injured, he added. The strikes also caused fires ‌and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people, mayor Igor Terekhov said. In ‌Russian-controlled Luhansk, three ⁠people ​were ⁠killed ⁠in ​a Ukrainian ‌attack, said Russian-installed ‌authorities of ​the ⁠eastern Ukrainian ​region.

The summit of the coalition of the willing on Thursday was co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, Britain and France shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. China, Russia and the US said after their talks they had agreed to a peace statement, but the declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine. The European coalition’s meeting in Berlin expressed indignation at the trilateral’s cosy optics, reports Rebecca Bailey. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks would “take place soon”, with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the US, Russia and Ukraine. Merz, speaking in Berlin, did not give a date and added that “we are looking for locations on neutral ground”, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location. British prime minister Andy Burnham said: “I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter.”

A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged the historic Saint Volodymyr Cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. “Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day ... At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

articles.title: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’
articles.summary: Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal
body: Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China.

The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says.

But the Congressional Budget Office has evaluated the impact of Aukus, releasing detailed analysis on Friday morning, finding “the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy’s demand for submarines”.
“Increasing production further to replace SSNs [attack submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the Navy and the shipyards are facing,” the report found.
“The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the Navy for many years.”
Related: Aukus is ‘worst, riskiest and most costly’ Australian defence decision ever, public inquiry into submarine deal says
Under the so-called “Pillar One” of Aukus, the US has agreed to sell between three and five in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032.
The CBO analysis questioned whether any submarines transferred to Australia could be utilised in the event of a US conflict with China.
“Would China be less deterred if the United States reduced the number of its attack submarines to help Australia develop its own submarine force?”

The report argued that because of the longstanding, and robust, alliance between the US and Australia, boosting the Australian navy’s submarine fleet could help offset the US Navy’s “potential loss of capability”.

“That loss might even be more than offset because the Australian submarines would be based in the Western Pacific region and therefore could respond more quickly to any conflict with China over Taiwan or other issues in the South China Sea.
“However, Australia would control its own submarines, and their participation in any particular conflict would not be guaranteed.”

In 2023, Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said Australia would make no promises it would deploy its submarines in support of any US conflict with China, and that any future Australian submarines would be “under the complete control of the Australian government of the day”.

Submarine-building rates in the US have been tenaciously laggard. The country’s shipyards are currently producing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.13 a year: that rate needs to lift that to two submarines a year to service America’s own needs, and 2.33 a year to have additional boats to transfer to Australia.
The CBO report said submarine-building rates had slowed over the past two decades, and Virginia-class submarines were delayed between 24 and 36 months.
“Building … submarines took five to six years in the 2000s but now takes an average of 10 to 11 years, according to current schedules.”

The US legislation governing Aukus states that the president of the US can only transfer a submarine to Australia if losing that submarine from US service “will not degrade the United States undersea capabilities”.
The US can refuse to transfer any submarines to Australia without penalty, under the terms of the Aukus agreement.
Related: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal
Critics of Aukus have said there is vanishingly little chance the US will have the capacity to sell any of its in-service submarines to Australia.

The former foreign affairs minister Bob Carr told Guardian Australia both countries were “living a lie” in upholding the fiction that the submarine deal would happen. “It’s now conventional wisdom in Washington as well as in Canberra that we’re not going to get the subs.”

But the deal has avowed, bipartisan broad political support across both the US and Australia. Marles said earlier this month: “Aukus is happening, our alliance is happening, and all of that continues unimpeded.”

Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, affirmed his support for the Aukus agreement, and the two countries’ commitment “to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific” at a meeting with Marles in September.
The US Congressional Research Service has openly countenanced an “alternative division of labour” under which no Virginia-class submarines are ever transferred to Australian control.

The research service’s latest report on Aukus, issued in January, considered a revision of the Aukus deal under which the submarines earmarked for sale to Australia were instead retained under US command to be sailed out of Australian bases.

The report argued both for and against the US selling three Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032. But it makes the case that, in the event of a “conflict or crisis” with China over Taiwan, submarines under Australian command could not be ordered into operation, whereas US-commanded vessels, operated out of Australian bases, could be immediately deployed.

articles.title: Putin vows ‘painful’ response to Ukraine’s bombing of Kerch bridge
articles.summary: Russian president makes remarks after Ukraine strikes strategic bridge to Crimea for third time in a week
body: Vladimir Putin has said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea will be “painful”, after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week.

The warning was delivered at a press conference after Putin met Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China. The Russian president claimed he had been considering agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed.

“After the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not negotiate,” Putin said, insisting the bridge was used only by civilians. “We will respond to these attacks. Our response will be far more painful than Kyiv’s attack on the bridge.”

A series of explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital in the mid-afternoon, and there were reports that a Russian drone had struck near the Dutch embassy in Kyiv, though it was unclear if it was deliberately targeted.

Shortly after midnight on Tuesday, Ukraine’s military blew up the central span of the Kerch road bridge in a complex air raid that involved Ruta cruise missiles made by a Dutch company as well as several Ukrainian cruise missiles and drones.

Russia threatened the Netherlands afterwards, with the Russian embassy in the country asking: “Is the Dutch government openly taking part in the conflict?” after the company, Destinus, had said it was a key element in the attack.

Tom Berendsen, the Dutch foreign minister, confirmed that “a projectile struck behind” the embassy in Kyiv. “Fortunately, our colleagues are unharmed, though there is some minor damage to the building,” he said, adding that officials were now investigating the incident.
A 26-year-old man had been killed and five others injured in the afternoon attacks, city authorities said.

Ukrainian military sources said the destruction of the Kerch bridge had been deliberately timed to embarrass Putin before the extraordinary summit, in which the Russian president sat down with Trump and Xi to discuss the war and other issues.

After his talks with Putin, Trump dialled into a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies in Berlin, during which he reportedly asked why European countries continued to spend billions on military support for Kyiv and said Putin was ready to negotiate a peace deal.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, when asked at a press conference whether Trump was painting too optimistic a picture of Russia’s desire for peace, said: “Too rosy a picture? No, certainly not. That was not the phone call that we heard from the president this afternoon. I would say quite the opposite, to be honest.”

Ukraine followed up Tuesday’s bombing of the Kerch bridge with a further attack on the remaining rail bridge to Crimea on Wednesday night. Train services were halted as a result of the strikes, which Ukraine’s military said were conducted with Neptune missiles made in Ukraine.

Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.
Emergency repair workers had made “heroic efforts” to restore the track, the governor said. Nobody was reported wounded as a result of the incident, Russia’s transport ministry added.

Ukraine’s military said the Kerch bridge was “the main land artery the Russian army uses to supply its occupation groupings in the south with fuel, ammunition and equipment” – in contrast to the comments made by Putin.

The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) bridge, built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea, has been struck three times in a week. Initial attacks on Monday had shown that Tuesday’s full-scale assault would be possible.
A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait collapsed into the Sea of Azov after a complex air raid that had been prepared and planned over several weeks.

A source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” they said.
Related: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play

For Ukraine, the bridge across the Kerch strait is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried to blow it up twice in the past – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack this week as the culmination of a seven-stage campaign to demolish the bridge, largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles, clearing the radar and air defences of Russian-occupied Ukraine.
Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central section of the bridge, bringing down its supporting arch.

articles.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.summary: Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
body: China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
Related: ‘Really making history’: five takeaways from the meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Related: ‘End your war, end it now’: Anthony Albanese tells Vladimir Putin to put a stop to Ukraine war

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
articles.summary: Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda
body: It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.

Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea, the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.

The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping. As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.

From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.

For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China, the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.

The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and the USSR sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”

Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.

Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.
Related: Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting

It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.

By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.

Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”

It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.
For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

articles.title: Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
articles.summary: No breakthroughs on major subjects at first trilateral summit between leaders of US, China and Russia
body: The presidents of the US, China and Russia met on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral gathering on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. The session lasted more than an hour and Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin touched on nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine and wider international security.

The trio lead the world’s three major nuclear powers and their decisions have far-reaching consequences for global security. However, their meeting in China ended without an announced breakthrough or concrete agreement on the main issues. Here are five key takeaways:

Trump opened the talks by telling Xi and Putin that “we are really making history”. He described the US, China and Russia as “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles and lowering the risk of such weapons being used.

It was an unusually high-profile display of cooperation between three countries whose relations have been marked by significant tensions, especially over Ukraine, trade disputes and the Nvidia scandal.
Trump also argued that peace could not be achieved by turning down opportunities for dialogue. It was the first time the leaders of the three countries had held a trilateral summit of this kind.

The talks came against the backdrop of the New Start nuclear agreement expiring in February. The treaty limits the arsenals of the US and Russia, capping each side at 1,550 deployed strategic nuclear warheads.
In September last year, Putin proposed voluntarily maintaining these limits for another year, but Trump rejected that approach, calling instead for a new agreement that would include China.

In the meeting on Thursday, Xi called for every effort to be made to prevent nuclear war and for nuclear weapons to be “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed”. However, no new arms control agreement was announced.
Related: What is Apec - explained in 30 seconds

Putin told Trump and Xi that their countries had “many converging interests” when it came to resolving conflicts, explicitly mentioning the war in Ukraine. He also spoke of their shared responsibility for international peace and security.

Like Putin, Trump arrived at the meeting fighting a failing war of choice. The Iran conflict has become an increasingly uncertain and costly undertaking for the US with no clear end in sight, while Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, continues to exact a heavy toll.
The meeting offered little indication of progress toward ending the war in Ukraine, and Kyiv was not mentioned in the subsequent joint peace declaration.
Trump described the international criminal court as “out of control”, criticising what he regards as the court’s excessive overreach.

His remarks carry particular significance given that Putin is wanted by the ICC on charges of war crimes. The court issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023, accusing him of unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.
The US and China are not signatories to the Rome statute, the international treaty that established the court, and are not bound by a requirement for member states to carry out its arrest warrants.
A joint “peace declaration” issued after the meeting by Chinese and Russian state media called for UN reform “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”.
The statement said the shake-up would range from boosting fuel supplies to engaging in “dialogue to reduce nuclear risks”.
The US and China are already permanent members of the UN security council, each with veto powers. They, and Russia, have argued for a greater role for nations from Asia, Africa and South America.

Russia has openly opposed permanent security council bids from Germany and Japan, arguing that western and Nato countries are already overrepresented and vote as a single bloc against Russian interests.

The declaration also took aim at the ICC, saying the court and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction”. It emphasised state consent and respect for the immunity of officials, which could be interpreted as a challenge to the legal basis for the ICC’s arrest warrant for Putin.

articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules
articles.summary: Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes
body: Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.

One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”

Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.

After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.

The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.
Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.

The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the ​lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.

“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

The US state department said in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.
It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.

The Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

articles.title: Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza
articles.summary: First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu
body: The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.
The operation lasted about 24 hours and on Thursday the military said it had been “completed”.

The IDF ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.
Related: Children at risk as ‘weaponisation of aid’ surges in conflict zones, analysis finds

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

After the statement from the IDF that it had concluded the tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel, the defence ministry’s body in charge of civilian affairs in Palestinian territories, Cogat, said Palestinians would again be free to move in the targeted areas near al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.
Related: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry determined that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. A previous report by the commission in September 2025 found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited those acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

articles.title: Eight injured after driver in Israel repeatedly rams car into Palestinians
articles.summary: Arab MPs accuse politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards Palestinians at four locations in Kafr Qasim
body: Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.

Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.

Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and said: “As of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”

The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.

Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”

Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”. “Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”

In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver had first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.
